concept: Priority fee estimation APIs and landing probability
summary: Source-anchored research for Priority fee estimation APIs and landing probability. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Solana prices contention per piece of state (local fee markets). Transactions compete when they write the same account, so a hotspot raises fees only for transactions touching it. A blanket high fee during network-wide congestion is therefore often wasted on uncontested accounts. (high confidence)

When account keys are passed, Agave returns for each slot the larger of the block minimum and the highest minimum fee recorded for any of those writable accounts (a std::cmp::max over per-account minimums). An account's minimum is kept only if it exceeds the block minimum, and only writable accounts are tracked. Agave's own struct comment calls this 'the minimum fee needed to land a transaction'. Chainstack draws the practical consequence: each returned value is a floor, so an average or median of the values is an average or median floor, not the fee actually paid. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Solana prices contention per writable account, not network-wide. Transactions compete when they write the same account, so a hot account raises fees only for transactions that touch it. Agave's cache records minimum fees per writable account. Helius docs say 'Solana prices priority fees per writable account'. RPC Fast and OrbitFlare tell builders to estimate from the accounts their transaction writes, not from network-wide medians. A blanket high fee during network-wide congestion is therefore often wasted on uncontested accounts. (high confidence)

Handle retries on the client. Rebroadcast the same signed bytes every couple of seconds until the transaction confirms or its blockhash expires, and track lastValidBlockHeight (Triton: the transaction can land up to lastValidBlockHeight + 1). Do not re-sign with a new blockhash until getBlockHeight is above that value and getSignatureStatuses shows the original absent, because both signed versions can execute. Treat a transaction as landed at confirmed or finalized, since a processed transaction can be dropped on a minority fork. Triton says maxRetries has no effect on its endpoints. QuickNode and Chainstack suggest maxRetries 0 with your own rebroadcast loop. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Common estimation mistakes named by vendors: using a global network-wide estimate (Helius: paying a global VeryHigh 'usually means overpaying by a wide margin'; OrbitFlare: wrong for contested accounts and costly on quiet ones); cranking a blanket fee during 'network congestion' when the contention is local (RPC Fast); keeping library-default compute limits, which inflate the fee and, per OrbitFlare, rank the transaction lower with the scheduler; fixed fees that go stale within hours; and bidding to fix delivery for a transaction that never reaches the leader. (medium confidence)

Triton's getRecentPrioritizationFees accepts a 'percentile' integer from 1 to 10,000 (5000 = median; 0.01% to 100.00%). Values above 10,000 are rejected, and omitting it returns the standard minimum. For each of up to 150 recent blocks it returns the percentile of compute-unit prices paid by non-vote transactions. With account addresses it takes that percentile over the transactions that write-lock each account and returns the highest of those values. The client still has to aggregate the per-slot values. The example client makes two parallel calls, with and without percentile, so it falls back to the standard result on other providers. The method is a Triton extension that needs a validator patch (tag v1.17.23-getrpf of rpcpool/solana-public), and the example repo calls it 'currently in beta testing'. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Stake-weighted QoS and priority fees act at different stages. SWQoS governs whether and how early a transaction reaches the leader (ingress). Priority fees only order transactions already inside the leader's queue (banking stage). So a high fee cannot rescue a transaction that was shed before it arrived. (high confidence)

Dropped transactions are often not a fee problem. RPC Fast ranks the priority fee last in its checks, after blockhash freshness (about 150 blocks), compute-limit accuracy and the submission path. Triton adds that a 'processed' transaction can still be dropped on a minority fork and that the client must rebroadcast the same signed transaction until it confirms or its blockhash expires. (medium confidence)

Landing and success are different things. Helius (undated, data to Dec 2024) reports that 41.2% of non-vote transactions reverted in Dec 2024 (peak 75.7% in Apr 2024), with bots sending over 100,000 transactions a day accounting for 95.2% of reverts. A transaction that lands can still fail. (low confidence) (verified as of 2024-12-31)

The stock getRecentPrioritizationFees returns a per-slot minimum, not a market price. In Agave, a block's value is the lowest compute-unit price among the non-vote transactions that landed in it. Zero-price transactions count toward that minimum, because update() has no zero check. Vote transactions and transactions with a zero compute-unit limit are skipped, and only the optimistically confirmed bank's data is kept. The cache holds the last 150 blocks (MAX_NUM_RECENT_BLOCKS = 150). One unprioritised transaction in a slot therefore pins that slot's value at 0. Triton calls the result 'often zero' and Helius calls it 'relatively limited in its usefulness'. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Do not use VeryHigh or UnsafeMax as a routine fee or as a network statistic. Helius says both are 'deliberately tail-weighted' and not outlier-trimmed, that a single extreme bid anywhere in the lookback window sets UnsafeMax, and that UnsafeMax 'regularly reaches billions of micro-lamports per compute unit'. OrbitFlare advises a hard per-transaction cap so a contested launch cannot bid a bot into a loss. (medium confidence)

The reference implementations already handle v1. Agave's cache reads a version-neutral transaction configuration (priority_fee_lamports and compute_unit_limit), skips simple votes, skips any transaction whose compute_unit_limit is 0 ('its priority fee amount is not instructive'), and stores a per-unit price from compute_unit_price_in_microlamports(), with a rounding note in the code. Helius's Atlas README says v1 transactions are priced from the total priority fee divided by the compute-unit limit (capped at 1,400,000), the API response combines all versions, and metrics report legacy/v0 and v1 separately. Only these two implementations were checked. The production Helius, QuickNode and Triton services were not. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

The same account list can give different numbers, because providers combine accounts differently. Agave's stock method starts from the block minimum and takes the maximum with each supplied account's minimum. Triton takes the requested percentile over the transactions that write-lock each account and returns the highest of those values. Helius's Atlas code has two variants: v1 pools the transactions of all requested accounts into one group, and v2 keeps one group per account. Both then take the higher of the account-level and network-wide percentile at each level. Chainstack and OrbitFlare both state a cap of 128 account addresses for the stock method. That limit was not confirmed in Agave source. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Ingress limits act before fee ordering, and some providers tie fee level to routing. Everstake says low-stake connections drop packets before any fee comparison happens, so a sender paying ten times the average priority fee can still lose. QuickNode's docs say non-duplicate transactions sent with its recommended priority fee or higher are routed through its staked (SWQoS) connection, so at that provider the fee level is also a routing switch. Triton sends over a staked connection by default on mainnet. Chorus One says it cannot fully separate inclusion time from swQoS use in its data. A fee-versus-landing correlation measured through such a provider therefore mixes scheduler ordering with path quality. That conclusion is an inference. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Helius counts non-vote transactions that set no compute unit price as zero-fee samples. This is why Min and Low often return 0 and why Helius numbers sit below percentiles computed over priced transactions only. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-06)

Estimate scope decides usefulness. With neither a serialized transaction nor writable accountKeys, Helius returns a global estimate, which it says is not a fee to pay. Passing the writable accounts scopes the estimate to the local market you compete in. Practitioner guides likewise say to base the fee on the accounts the transaction touches, not on network-wide medians. (medium confidence)

A higher priority fee raises ordering priority but does not guarantee inclusion. Helius says the scheduler gives no guarantee, Chorus One found no fee threshold above which transactions consistently landed faster, and OrbitFlare says the fee only orders transactions while the submission path gets them to the leader. (medium confidence)

Landing-rate comparisons are easily distorted. RPC Fast says to hold the fee, transaction shape and commitment level constant across paths, count at one commitment level, and divide confirmed sends by all attempts including failures. It also says a path tested at a higher fee can look faster without being so. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-30)
